title: How to review your deep work without a distraction blocker
summary: Review a planned focus block against your calendar and work history, then choose one practical change for next week.
body_markdown:
A weekly work review helps you compare the time you planned with the work you remember doing. Set aside ten minutes, bring your calendar and work record, and choose one adjustment to try next week.


You do not need to assign every minute a productivity score. A long block of app usage does not prove you were concentrating, and a short break does not mean the day went badly.


## Review one planned focus block


Start with a specific block from your calendar. Write down the task you intended to work on, then compare it with your notes or activity timeline.


- Did you make progress on the intended task? Check the document, issue, or other output.
- Did a meeting or urgent request change the plan? Add that context before judging the result.
- Was there time you cannot account for? Leave it uncertain rather than treating it as wasted time.


[Dayflow](https://www.dayflow.so/) can help you reconstruct screen-based activity on Mac. Its AI timeline is a starting point for this review, not a measurement of attention. Correct any entries that misread what you were doing and add work that happened away from the screen.


## Make one change you can check


For example, suppose a planned writing block was interrupted by two scheduled calls. You might move writing to a meeting-free morning next week. If messages interrupted it, try closing the messaging app for that block, provided your work allows it.


Keep a short note:


> Planned: draft the proposal on Tuesday morning. What happened: two calls split the time. Next week: reserve Wednesday morning and check whether the first draft gets finished.


This example is illustrative. The useful part is that you can check the change against a specific outcome next week.


## When a blocker helps


A review helps you decide what to change; a blocker can help you follow that decision during a work session. Dayflow does not block distractions. If that is a requirement, compare the[focus tools and work journals in our RescueTime guide](https://www.dayflow.so/compare/rescuetime-alternative/) .


Dayflow keeps full recordings and the local timeline on your Mac. Local AI keeps screenshot analysis on-device, while cloud modes send selected screenshots for analysis. Read the[privacy explanation](https://www.dayflow.so/blog/is-dayflow-safe/) before setting it up.


If you need to communicate the week’s progress, turn the reviewed record into a[status update](https://www.dayflow.so/blog/automatic-standup-updates/) . Keep your personal activity details out of the shared version.
